domain_symbols.matrix_real: real matrices and vectors used to represent systems

rules.name: System solution means simultaneous satisfaction
rules.input_form: equation system and assignment
rules.output_form: assignment is a solution iff every equation is true simultaneously
preconditions: The assignment is defined for every system variable
rules.operation: Interpret a system solution as a simultaneous truth assignment for all equations.
examples: If a pair satisfies one equation but not the other, it is not a system solution
counterexamples: Solving equations independently and keeping incompatible assignments is invalid

rules.name: Linear equation form
rules.input_form: a1x1 + ... + anxn = b
preconditions: Variables do not multiply each other and appear only to first power
rules.operation: Recognize an equation as linear in its variables.
examples: 2x + 3y = 7 is linear
counterexamples: xy = 1 is not linear
x^2 + y = 4 is not linear

rules.name: Replace an equation by an equivalent equation
rules.input_form: system with one equation replaced by an equivalent equation
preconditions: The replacement equation is logically equivalent to the original equation in the active domain
rules.operation: Preserve the solution set by replacing an equation with an equivalent one.
examples: Replacing 2x = 8 with x = 4 preserves solutions
counterexamples: Replacing an equation with a nonequivalent statement changes the solution set

rules.name: Row-style combination rule
rules.input_form: system where one equation is replaced by itself plus a multiple of another
preconditions: The multiplier is defined in the active domain
rules.operation: Add a multiple of one equation to another without changing the solution set.
examples: From x + y = 3 and x - y = 1, subtracting the second from the first yields 2y = 2
counterexamples: Applying different uncontrolled transformations to both equations can break equivalence

rules.name: Isolate a variable in a simple equation
rules.input_form: linear equation with one easily isolated variable
rules.output_form: equivalent explicit expression for that variable
preconditions: The target variable has a nonzero coefficient and isolation is straightforward
rules.operation: Solve one equation for one variable in preparation for substitution.
examples: x + y = 3 becomes x = 3 - y
counterexamples: Isolating incorrectly, such as x = 3 + y, is invalid

rules.name: Substitute into remaining equations
rules.input_form: system and isolated variable expression
rules.output_form: reduced system with one fewer variable in a target equation
preconditions: The isolated expression is equivalent to the original equation
rules.operation: Replace the isolated variable in the remaining equations by its equivalent expression.
examples: Substituting x = 3 - y into x - y = 1 gives 3 - y - y = 1
counterexamples: Substituting into only part of an equation is invalid

rules.name: Back-substitution
rules.input_form: solved value for one variable and an earlier relation
preconditions: The earlier relation remains valid for the current system
rules.operation: Recover remaining variable values after solving for one variable.
examples: After finding y = 1, substitute into x + y = 3 to get x = 2
counterexamples: Reporting a partial assignment as a complete solution is invalid

rules.name: Align variables for elimination
rules.input_form: two equations with a target elimination variable
rules.output_form: scaled or arranged equations with opposite coefficients
preconditions: The target variable appears in both equations with controllable coefficients
rules.operation: Prepare a pair of equations so a chosen variable will cancel under addition or subtraction.
examples: x + y = 3 and x - y = 1 already align for eliminating y by addition
counterexamples: Eliminating mismatched variables without coefficient control is invalid

rules.name: Eliminate a variable by addition or subtraction
rules.input_form: aligned equations
rules.output_form: reduced equation with one fewer variable
preconditions: A chosen variable has opposite or matching coefficients suitable for cancellation
rules.operation: Combine equations so one variable cancels.
examples: Adding x + y = 3 and x - y = 1 gives 2x = 4
counterexamples: Combining equations and failing to cancel correctly is invalid

rules.name: Solve reduced equation and recover remaining variables
rules.input_form: single-variable reduced equation and original system relation
preconditions: The reduced equation was derived equivalently from the original system
rules.operation: Solve the reduced equation, then back-substitute into an original or equivalent relation.
examples: 2x = 4 gives x = 2, then x + y = 3 gives y = 1
counterexamples: Recovering remaining variables from a transformed equation that lost needed information can be invalid

rules.name: Coefficient matrix representation
rules.input_form: linear system
preconditions: The system is linear
rules.operation: Represent a linear system in matrix-vector form.
examples: The system 2x + y = 5 and x - y = 1 corresponds to A = [[2,1],[1,-1]]
counterexamples: Non-linear systems do not fit this linear matrix form directly

rules.name: Augmented matrix representation
rules.input_form: coefficient matrix A and constant vector b
preconditions: The ordering of variables is fixed consistently
rules.operation: Attach the constant column to the coefficient matrix for row-operation workflows.
examples: [A|b] stores the system in row-operation form
counterexamples: Mixing coefficient and constant columns incorrectly changes the system

rules.name: Unique solution case
rules.input_form: reduced system
preconditions: Reduction yields one value for each variable and no free variables
rules.operation: Classify the system as having a unique solution.
examples: x + y = 3 and x - y = 1 has unique solution (2,1)
counterexamples: Free variables indicate the solution is not unique

rules.name: Inconsistent system case
rules.input_form: reduced system with contradiction row
preconditions: Reduction yields a contradiction such as 0 = 5
rules.operation: Classify the system as inconsistent.
examples: x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 are inconsistent together
counterexamples: Treating a contradiction row as harmless is invalid

rules.name: Infinitely many solutions case
rules.input_form: reduced system with dependent equations and free variables
preconditions: At least one free variable remains and no contradiction is present
rules.operation: Classify the system as having infinitely many solutions.
examples: x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 4 have infinitely many solutions
counterexamples: Claiming uniqueness when a free parameter remains is invalid

rules.name: Invalid equation-by-equation solution merge
rules.input_form: independent equation solutions merged without simultaneous check
rules.operation: Mark independent solution merging without simultaneous validation as invalid.
counterexamples: Values valid for one equation but not the other are not system solutions

rules.name: Invalid elimination arithmetic
rules.input_form: equations combined without coefficient alignment or correct arithmetic
rules.operation: Mark naive elimination without compatible coefficients or correct arithmetic as invalid.
counterexamples: x + 2y = 5 and x + y = 3 do not cancel y by naive subtraction unless arithmetic is done correctly

rules.name: Gaussian elimination step
rules.input_form: matrix row set or equation system with pivot row
rules.output_form: equivalent system with zeros introduced below a pivot
preconditions: A pivot entry has been chosen
The applied row operation is valid
rules.operation: Use a valid row operation to eliminate entries below a pivot and move the system toward echelon form.
examples: Subtracting 2 times the first row from the second can eliminate a leading coefficient below the pivot
counterexamples: Changing only part of a row is invalid

rules.name: Read solution from row-echelon form
rules.input_form: row-echelon or reduced-row-echelon system
preconditions: The system has been reduced to echelon form
rules.operation: Solve pivot variables from the bottom upward and identify any free variables.
examples: If the last row gives y = 1 and the row above gives x + y = 3, then x = 2
counterexamples: Reading a free variable as uniquely determined is invalid

rules.name: Nonzero determinant implies unique solution
rules.input_form: square system Ax = b
preconditions: A is square
det(A) != 0
rules.operation: Use a nonzero determinant to conclude invertibility and uniqueness.
examples: A 2x2 system with determinant 5 has exactly one solution
counterexamples: Determinant reasoning in this form does not apply directly to nonsquare systems

rules.name: Zero determinant blocks inverse-based uniqueness
rules.input_form: square system Ax = b
preconditions: A is square
det(A) = 0
rules.operation: Use determinant zero to rule out inverse-based unique solving while leaving consistency to further analysis.
examples: Two proportional equations give determinant 0 and no inverse-based unique solution
counterexamples: Determinant 0 does not by itself decide between inconsistency and infinitely many solutions

rules.name: Least-squares normal equations
rules.input_form: overdetermined system Ax approximately equals b
preconditions: The least-squares formulation is active
Matrix products are well-defined
rules.operation: Translate an overdetermined least-squares problem into its normal equations.
examples: A line-fit problem reduces to normal equations for the coefficient vector
counterexamples: Treating an inconsistent overdetermined system as exactly solvable without approximation is invalid

rules.name: Inverse matrix solution rule
rules.input_form: Ax = b
preconditions: A is invertible
rules.operation: Solve a square system by left-multiplying with the inverse matrix.
examples: For invertible A, left-multiplying Ax = b by A^(-1) isolates x
counterexamples: Using A^(-1)b when A is singular is invalid

rules.name: Rank-based consistency check
rules.input_form: coefficient matrix A and augmented matrix [A|b]
preconditions: The ranks are computed correctly
rules.operation: Use rank equality or inequality between A and [A|b] to classify consistency and uniqueness structure.
examples: Equal coefficient and augmented ranks certify consistency
counterexamples: rank(A) < rank([A|b]) signals inconsistency, not a solution family

rules.name: Canonical form normalization expansion
rules.input_form: raw expression E
preconditions: Auto-expansion rule requires explicit domain assumptions and validation metadata
rules.operation: Rewrite expressions into a canonical form that preserves the active equivalence relation.
examples: x + y and y + x map to a shared canonical additive form in commutative settings
counterexamples: Applying canonicalization rules outside their preconditions is invalid
common_errors: Using auto-generated rules without confirming domain-specific assumptions
